questions.question: What is a linked list and how does it differ from an array?
questions.title: Linked List vs Array | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **linked list** is a chain of **nodes**, each holding a value and a **reference to the next node**, scattered across memory. Unlike an **array** (contiguous, O(1) random access), a linked list has **no index access** - reaching position k is O(k). Its win is **O(1) insert/delete at a known node** (just relink pointers), versus O(n) shifting in an array. Arrays also cache better.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can articulate the access-vs-modify tradeoff and the memory layout difference
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying linked lists are 'always faster for insertion' without the 'at a known position' caveat, or claiming O(1) random access
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention cache locality (arrays win) and that O(1) insert assumes you already hold the node reference

sections.title: Linked List vs Array: Memory and Access
sections.content:
A **linked list** stores elements as **nodes** scattered in memory; each node holds a value and a **reference (pointer) to the next node**. The list only knows its **head**. An **array** stores elements in one **contiguous block**, so element `i` is found by address arithmetic.

The core tradeoff: arrays give **O(1) random access** by index but **O(n) insert/delete in the middle** (everything shifts). Linked lists give **no random access** - reaching position k means walking k pointers (**O(k)**) - but **O(1) insert/delete** once you hold the node, since you just relink pointers. Arrays also benefit from **cache locality** (contiguous memory is prefetched), which often makes them faster in practice.

sections.title: Array vs Linked List
sections.content:
blue|Array|~contiguous block|O(1) index access|O(n) middle insert|great cache locality
amber|Linked list|~scattered nodes|O(k) to reach k|O(1) relink insert|extra pointer per node
emerald|Array wins|~random access + cache|read-heavy workloads|known fixed size|sorting, binary search
rose|Linked wins|~frequent splice|insert/delete at node|no shifting|unknown/growing size

sections.title: Array - O(n) middle insert (shift)
Linked list - O(1) relink at a known node
When to Use Each
sections.content:
- **Array / ArrayList**: random access by index, read-heavy work, sorting, binary search, or when size is roughly known. Default choice in Java.
- **LinkedList**: frequent inserts/deletes at the ends or at a held position, building queues/deques, or when you never need index access.
- In practice, `ArrayList` wins most of the time due to cache locality; `LinkedList` shines for `Deque`/queue use via `ArrayDeque`-style patterns.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Linked list = **nodes + next pointers**, scattered; array = **contiguous**.
- Array: **O(1) access**, O(n) middle insert. Linked list: **O(k) access**, O(1) relink.
- O(1) insert assumes you **already hold the node**.
- Arrays have **better cache locality** (often faster in practice).
- Linked nodes cost **extra memory** for the pointer(s).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A linked list is a chain of nodes, where each node holds a value and a reference to the next node, and the list itself only knows about its head. The nodes can be scattered anywhere in memory; they're connected purely by those references. An array, by contrast, stores all its elements in one contiguous block of memory, so element i is located by simple address arithmetic. That difference drives the whole tradeoff. Arrays give O of one random access: I can jump straight to any index. But inserting or deleting in the middle is O of n, because everything after the spot has to shift over. Linked lists are the opposite. They have no random access at all, so reaching position k means walking k pointers from the head, which is O of k. But once I'm holding a particular node, inserting or deleting is O of one, because I just relink a couple of pointers and nothing shifts. The important caveat I always add is that the O of one insertion assumes I already have a reference to the node; if I have to find it first, that search is still O of n. I'd also mention cache locality. Because arrays are contiguous, the CPU prefetches nearby elements, so array traversal is often noticeably faster in practice than chasing scattered pointers. And each linked-list node costs extra memory for its pointer. So in real Java code I default to ArrayList, and I reach for a linked structure mainly for queue or deque patterns with lots of end insertions.

questions.question: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
questions.title: Detect Cycle in Linked List | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Floyd's tortoise-and-hare**: move `slow` one node and `fast` two nodes each step. If they ever meet, the list has a **cycle**; if `fast` reaches `null`, it doesn't. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space. To find the cycle's **start**, reset one pointer to the head after they meet and advance both one step at a time until they meet again.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you reach for Floyd's O(1)-space detection and can extend it to find the cycle start
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using O(n)-space HashSet, or NPE from not guarding fast.next
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Add the bonus: resetting to head finds the entry point of the loop

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Floyd's: slow +1, fast +2; **meeting = cycle**.
- **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.
- `fast == null` -> no cycle.
- **Reset to head + step both** -> finds the **cycle start**.
- Compare references; guard against null.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: I'd use Floyd's cycle detection, the tortoise and hare. I start two pointers at the head, then move slow one node per step and fast two nodes per step. If the list is acyclic, fast eventually reaches null and I return that there's no cycle. If there is a cycle, both pointers enter the loop, and because fast gains one position on slow every step, the gap between them shrinks to zero and they're guaranteed to meet on the same node. That meeting is my proof of a cycle, and it's O of n time with O of one space, which beats the HashSet approach that costs O of n space. The part that really impresses interviewers is finding where the cycle begins. After the two pointers meet, I reset one of them, say slow, back to the head, and then I advance both pointers one node at a time. The node where they meet the second time is the start of the cycle. That falls out of the distance relationship: the distance from the head to the loop entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the loop entry, going around. I won't derive the full math unless asked, but I know the procedure. Two implementation details: I guard the loop with fast not null and fast dot next not null so I don't dereference null when stepping fast twice, and I compare node references with double equals, not their values, because duplicate values don't imply a cycle.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A **linked list** is a chain of **nodes**, each holding a value and a **reference to the next node**, scattered across memory.

Unlike an **array** (contiguous, O(1) random access), a linked list has **no index access** - reaching position k is O(k).

Its win is **O(1) insert/delete at a known node** (just relink pointers), versus O(n) shifting in an array. Arrays also cache better.

Saying linked lists are 'always faster for insertion' without the 'at a known position' caveat, or claiming O(1) random access

sections.title: Detect, Then Locate the Loop Start
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[slow=fast=head] --> B{fast and fast.next?} B -- no --> N[no cycle] B -- yes --> C[slow+=1, fast+=2] C --> D{slow == fast?} D -- no --> B D -- yes --> E[meeting point] E --> F[reset slow=head
advance both by 1] F --> G[meet again =
cycle start] ```

sections.title: Detect Cycle + Find Start (Dry Run)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **HashSet of visited**: O(n) space when Floyd's gives O(1).
- **NPE**: guard `fast != null && fast.next != null`.
- **Comparing values**: compare node **references**.
- **Skipping the reset proof**: know the meeting->head reset finds the cycle start.

questions.question: How do you reverse a singly linked list in Java?
questions.title: Reverse Linked List Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Reverse the `next` pointers in place using three references - `prev`, `curr`, `next`. For each node: save `next`, set `curr.next = prev`, then move `prev` and `curr` forward. The new head is `prev` when `curr` hits `null`. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space. A recursive version is shorter but uses O(n) stack space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write the in-place pointer-reversal and choose iterative (O(1) space) over recursive
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overwriting curr.next before saving the next node, or returning head instead of prev
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast iterative O(1) space with recursive O(n) stack space and return prev as the new head

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Iterative: **prev/curr/next**, save -> flip -> advance.
- New head = **prev** when `curr == null`.
- **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space iterative.
- Recursive is shorter but **O(n)** stack space.
- Order of operations is the crux - save before flipping.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: To reverse a singly linked list in Java, the approach I prefer is iterative and in place, using three references: prev, curr, and a temporary next. Prev starts as null and curr starts at the head. I walk through the list, and for each node I do four steps in a careful order. First I save curr dot next into next, so I don't lose the rest of the list once I rewire the pointer. Then I flip the link by setting curr dot next to prev. Then I advance prev to curr and curr to next. When curr becomes null, every node has been flipped, and prev is now pointing at the original last node, which is the new head, so I return prev. This is one pass, O of n time, and O of one space because I'm only juggling a few pointers. I'd also mention there's a recursive version, which is quite elegant: you recurse to the end, then on the way back you set head dot next dot next to head and head dot next to null. It's clean and shows good understanding, but it uses O of n stack space because of all the nested calls, and on a very long list it can even overflow the stack. So for an in-place, constant-space reversal I go with the iterative version. The two mistakes I consciously avoid are flipping curr dot next before I've saved the next node, which strands the rest of the list, and returning the old head instead of prev, since the old head ends up as the tail.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
A **linked list** is a chain of **nodes**, each holding a value and a **reference to the next node**, scattered across memory.

Unlike an **array** (contiguous, O(1) random access), a linked list has **no index access** - reaching position k is O(k).

Its win is **O(1) insert/delete at a known node** (just relink pointers), versus O(n) shifting in an array. Arrays also cache better.

Saying linked lists are 'always faster for insertion' without the 'at a known position' caveat, or claiming O(1) random access

sections.title: Iterative Pointer Reversal
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[prev=null, curr=head] --> B{curr != null?} B -- no --> Z[return prev = new head] B -- yes --> C[next = curr.next] C --> D[curr.next = prev] D --> E[prev = curr
curr = next] E --> B ```

sections.title: Recursive - elegant but O(n) stack space
Iterative - O(1) space (preferred)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Flip before save**: setting `curr.next = prev` before storing `next` loses the tail.
- **Return head**: return **prev** (the old head is now the tail).
- **Recursive on long lists**: O(n) stack can overflow; prefer iterative.
- **Forgetting null start**: `prev` begins null so the old head ends at null.

questions.question: How do you find the middle element of a linked list?
questions.title: Find Middle of Linked List | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use the **slow/fast (tortoise-and-hare) pointers**. Move `slow` one node and `fast` two nodes per step; when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is at the **middle** - all in **one pass**, O(n) time, O(1) space. For an even-length list this lands on the **second** middle (use `fast.next != null` to stop earlier if you want the first).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the one-pass two-pointer trick instead of counting length then re-traversing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Doing two passes (count then walk to n/2), or mishandling even-length and null checks
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Control which middle you return for even lengths via the fast-pointer loop condition

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Slow +1, fast +2**; when fast ends, slow is the middle.
- **One pass**, O(n) time, O(1) space.
- Loop guard `fast != null && fast.next != null` avoids NPE.
- Even length: condition picks first vs **second** middle.
- Same two-speed idea powers cycle detection.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The clean way to find the middle of a linked list is the slow and fast pointer technique, sometimes called tortoise and hare. I start both pointers at the head. Then in each step I move the slow pointer one node forward and the fast pointer two nodes forward. The fast pointer covers ground twice as quickly, so by the time it reaches the end of the list, the slow pointer has only gone halfway, which means it's sitting right at the middle. That gives me the answer in a single pass, O of n time and O of one space. The alternative is to first count the length and then walk again to position length over two, but that's two passes, and the two-pointer version is what interviewers want. A couple of details I'm careful about. The loop condition has to be fast not null and fast dot next not null, checked before I move fast twice, otherwise I'll hit a null pointer exception when I try fast dot next dot next near the end. For an odd-length list, slow lands on the single, unambiguous middle. For an even-length list there are two middle nodes, and which one I return depends on my loop condition. With fast not null and fast dot next not null, I return the second middle; if I want the first, I tweak the condition. I'd also handle the empty list by returning null when head is null. And I'd point out this two-speed idea is the same trick used to detect cycles in a linked list.

Its win is **O(1) insert/delete at a known node** (just relink pointers), versus O(n) shifting in an array. Arrays also cache better.

Saying linked lists are 'always faster for insertion' without the 'at a known position' caveat, or claiming O(1) random access

Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Two passes**: counting then re-walking works but isn't the expected one-pass answer.
- **NPE on fast.next.next**: guard with `fast != null && fast.next != null` before stepping fast twice.
- **Even-length confusion**: be explicit about returning the first vs second middle.
- **Empty list**: handle `head == null` (return null).

questions.question: What is the difference between singly linked list and doubly linked list?
questions.title: Singly vs Doubly Linked List | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **singly linked list** node has one pointer (**next**), so traversal is forward-only and each node uses less memory. A **doubly linked list** node has two pointers (**next and prev**), enabling **backward traversal** and **O(1) deletion of a known node** (you can reach its predecessor directly) - at the cost of an extra pointer per node. Java's `LinkedList` is doubly linked.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the prev pointer enables backward traversal and O(1) node deletion
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking deletion is O(1) in a singly linked list (it needs the predecessor, which is O(n) to find)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why deleting a known node is O(1) in doubly but O(n) in singly (no back pointer)

sections.title: Singly vs Doubly Linked List
sections.content:
In a **singly linked list**, each node stores its value and a single **`next`** pointer. You can only move **forward**, and the list knows its `head`. In a **doubly linked list**, each node also stores a **`prev`** pointer, so you can traverse in **both directions**, and the list usually tracks both `head` and `tail`.

The practical payoff of `prev` is **O(1) deletion of a node you already hold**: in a singly list you must walk from the head to find the predecessor (**O(n)**) just to relink around the node, whereas a doubly list reaches the predecessor instantly. The cost is **extra memory** (one more pointer per node) and more bookkeeping on every insert/delete. Java's `java.util.LinkedList` is a doubly linked list.

sections.title: One Pointer vs Two
sections.content:
blue|Singly linked|~one next pointer|forward only|less memory per node|delete known node O(n)
amber|Doubly linked|~next and prev|both directions|extra pointer per node|delete known node O(1)
emerald|Doubly wins|~O(1) node delete|backward traversal|tail operations|LRU cache, deque
rose|Singly wins|~memory + simplicity|simple stacks|forward-only scans|less pointer upkeep

sections.title: Singly - deleting a known node needs the predecessor
Doubly - delete a known node in O(1)
When to Use Each
sections.content:
- **Singly**: memory-sensitive, forward-only use - simple stacks, hash-bucket chains, basic queues.
- **Doubly**: need backward traversal, O(1) deletion of held nodes, or a **deque** - e.g. an **LRU cache** (doubly linked list + HashMap) where you move/evict nodes in O(1).
- In Java, prefer `ArrayDeque` for plain stack/queue needs; `LinkedList` (doubly) when you specifically need node-level splicing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Singly = **next only** (forward); doubly = **next + prev** (both ways).
- Doubly enables **O(1) deletion of a known node**; singly is O(n) (find predecessor).
- Doubly costs **one extra pointer** per node.
- Java's `LinkedList` is **doubly linked**.
- Doubly powers **LRU caches** and **deques**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The difference comes down to how many pointers each node carries. In a singly linked list, every node has a value and a single next pointer, so I can only move forward through the list, and the list keeps track of its head. In a doubly linked list, each node has both a next and a previous pointer, so I can traverse in either direction, and the list usually tracks both the head and the tail. The most important practical consequence of that previous pointer is deletion. If I'm handed a node and asked to delete it, in a doubly linked list it's O of one, because I can immediately reach its predecessor through the prev pointer and relink both sides. In a singly linked list, I don't have a back pointer, so to delete a node I first have to walk from the head to find the node before it, which is O of n. That's a subtlety freshers often miss; they assume deletion is always O of one. The cost of the doubly linked list is memory and bookkeeping: an extra pointer per node, and every insert or delete has to maintain two links instead of one. Java's built-in LinkedList is actually a doubly linked list. Where doubly really shines is something like an LRU cache, which combines a doubly linked list with a HashMap so you can move a node to the front or evict from the back in constant time, and for deques where you add and remove at both ends. If I only need forward traversal and want to save memory, singly is simpler.
